answer.sourceLine: Hawking gave this as the closing answer of a long interview conducted at his Cambridge office by Klaus Franke and Henry Glass and printed in Der Spiegel, issue 42/1988. One caveat the quote sites never mention: the magazine printed the answer in German, so the polished English sentence everyone shares is a rendering of that text, not a transcript.

source.heading: The SPIEGEL-Gespräch, October 1988

docMeta.dd: »Wir alle wollen wissen, woher wir kommen« — SPIEGEL-Gespräch with Stephen Hawking
Der Spiegel, issue 42/1988 — dated 16 October 1988 on spiegel.de; Wikiquote cites 17 October 1988
Klaus Franke and Henry Glass, at Hawking's office in Cambridge
Printed in German. The familiar English sentence is an uncredited rendering; no English transcript located.

source.excerpt: SPIEGEL: Die Frage nach unserem Standort im Universum scheint Sie nahezu übermächtig zu beschäftigen. Haben Sie schon eine Antwort darauf? — HAWKING: Wir sind nur eine etwas fortgeschrittene Brut von Affen auf einem kleinen Planeten, der um einen höchst durchschnittlichen Stern kreist. Aber wir können das Universum verstehen, und das macht aus uns etwas sehr Besonderes.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ carries the line in its sourced section — not under Attributed or Misattributed — and cites Der Spiegel (17 October 1988). That gave us a publication and a week to check.
TIME ↗, in its 2018 collection of Hawking quotations, independently reports that he told it to “German paper Der Spiegel” in 1988.

The interview itself is online: »Wir alle wollen wissen, woher wir kommen« ↗, Der Spiegel 42/1988, by Klaus Franke and Henry Glass at Cambridge. The monkeys sentence is Hawking’s closing answer — in German. That confirms the attribution and, at the same time, shows the English wording is a rendering.

German quote sites carry only the first clause and no citation at all (zitate7.de ↗), and at least one English database dates the line to 1989 (The Quotations Page ↗) — the two ways this quote degrades in transit.
source.excerptNote: That is the last exchange of the interview, exactly as Der Spiegel printed it. Rendered literally: ‘We are only a somewhat advanced breed of apes on a small planet that orbits a very average star. But we can understand the universe, and that makes us something very special.’ The sentence in circulation is a smoother, uncredited version of the same words.

author.name: Stephen Hawking
author.kicker: The man who actually said it
author.heading: Stephen Hawking
author.metaLine: 1942–2018 · Theoretical physicist · Lucasian Professor of Mathematics, Cambridge, 1979–2009
author.bio: Stephen Hawking spent almost his whole career at Cambridge, holding the Lucasian Professorship of Mathematics from 1979 to 2009 and later directing research at the Centre for Theoretical Cosmology. Diagnosed with motor neurone disease as a young man, he did his work on black holes and the origin of the universe through decades of worsening paralysis, latterly speaking through a synthesiser. A Brief History of Time, published in 1988, made him the most famous scientist alive — which is why two editors from a German newsmagazine were sitting in his office that October.

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: Nobody else claims this line. The drift here is in the words and the date, not the name — and the most common distortion cuts the sentence that carries the whole point.

items.who: Stephen Hawking — right speaker, imported English
items.why: Der Spiegel printed the answer in German: “Wir sind nur eine etwas fortgeschrittene Brut von Affen auf einem kleinen Planeten, der um einen höchst durchschnittlichen Stern kreist. Aber wir können das Universum verstehen, und das macht aus uns etwas sehr Besonderes” (Der Spiegel 42/1988 ↗). Rendered literally that is ‘only a somewhat advanced breed of apes on a small planet that orbits a very average star’. The famous English drops the hedge and compresses the orbit into ‘a minor planet of a very average star’. No translator is credited anywhere, and rival English versions circulate — one site gives it as “a little advanced breed of monkeys on a small planet orbiting around a very average star” (Knowol ↗).

German-language quote sites routinely run the opening clause alone and stop — “Wir sind nur eine etwas fortgeschrittene Brut von Affen auf einem kleinen Planeten, der um einen höchst durchschnittlichen Stern kreist” with nothing after it (zitate7.de ↗). That leaves a bleak shrug where Hawking actually delivered a boast. The second half is the answer; the first half is only the setup.
The Quotations Page ↗ files the line under 1989. The interview ran in issue 42/1988; Wikiquote ↗ and TIME ↗ both put it in 1988.

misattribution.truthLine: Hawking really said it, as the last answer of a SPIEGEL-Gespräch in his Cambridge office (Der Spiegel 42/1988 ↗) — but he said it to a German magazine, and the sentence the internet quotes is an English rendering of the German they printed.

context.heading: Why he said it, and where
lead: It is autumn 1988 and Stephen Hawking is the most famous scientist on earth. A Brief History of Time, published earlier that year, is on the bestseller lists, and two editors from Der Spiegel, Klaus Franke and Henry Glass, have come to his office at Cambridge with a stenographer. The conversation ranges over the Big Bang, whether the universe’s beginning requires a creator, consciousness compared with computers, and what might become of the human race.

The monkeys line is not a stray aphorism dropped mid-conversation. It is the answer to the very last substantive question the magazine asks — whether Hawking has arrived at an answer about our place in the universe — which makes it a deliberate closing statement. And the whole force of it is in the turn: the humbling first half exists only to set up the second.
context.detailsSummary: A harsher cousin of the same image
detailsBody: Hawking used a blunter version of the same picture in 1995, on the television programme Reality on the Rocks: Beyond Our Ken, where he called the human race “a chemical scum on a moderate-sized planet, orbiting around a very average star” (Wikiquote ↗). Same cosmology, no consolation attached — which is worth knowing, because the two lines are often filed together and the 1988 one is the one with the redemptive second half.
context.pull: “But we can understand the Universe” — the half that keeps getting cut.

sourcesVerified.claim: Der Spiegel 42/1988 published the SPIEGEL-Gespräch »Wir alle wollen wissen, woher wir kommen« with Stephen Hawking, conducted by Klaus Franke and Henry Glass at his Cambridge office; its closing answer reads 'Wir sind nur eine etwas fortgeschrittene Brut von Affen auf einem kleinen Planeten, der um einen höchst durchschnittlichen Stern kreist. Aber wir können das Universum verstehen, und das macht aus uns etwas sehr Besonderes.' The page is timestamped 16.10.1988.

An English rendering of the same Der Spiegel page confirms the issue designation DER SPIEGEL 42/1988, the date 16.10.1988, the Politik rubric, the interviewers Klaus Franke and Henry Glass, and the closing answer about a somewhat advanced breed of apes on a small planet orbiting a very average star.

Wikiquote lists 'We are just an advanced breed of monkeys on a minor planet of a very average star. But we can understand the Universe. That makes us something very special.' in its sourced Quotes section, cited to Der Spiegel (17 October 1988); its Misattributed section lists only unrelated items, and it sources Hawking's 'chemical scum' line to Reality on the Rocks: Beyond Our Ken (1995).
TIME's collection of Hawking quotations prints the line and states that Hawking told it to German paper Der Spiegel in 1988.
The Quotations Page prints the same English wording but cites it to 'Der Spiegel, 1989', a year later than the issue in which the interview actually ran.

Knowol prints a competing English rendering — 'We are just a little advanced breed of monkeys on a small planet orbiting around a very average star. But we can understand the universe, and that makes us very special.' — citing the 17 October 1988 issue of Der Spiegel and linking to the spiegel.de article via Google Translate.

German quote aggregator zitate7.de carries only the first clause, 'Wir sind nur eine etwas fortgeschrittene Brut von Affen auf einem kleinen Planeten, der um einen höchst durchschnittlichen Stern kreist.', with no source citation and without the second half.

Wikipedia gives Stephen Hawking's dates as 8 January 1942 – 14 March 2018, records that he was Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at Cambridge from 1979 to 2009 and later director of research at the Centre for Theoretical Cosmology, and states that A Brief History of Time was published in April 1988 in the US and June 1988 in the UK.
German Wikiquote's Stephen Hawking page does not carry this quotation at all — no entry mentions 'Affen' or 'durchschnittlichen Stern' — so no German-language reference work independently sources it.
